(A) Clinical Diagnosis & Causative Organism (2 marks)

The clinical picture — chronic cough (≥2–4 weeks), low-grade evening fever, weight loss, loss of appetite, night sweats, haemoptysis (streaky or frank), and chest radiograph showing cavitary lesion typically in the right upper lobe (apical/posterior segments), with sputum showing acid-fast bacilli (AFB) — long, slender, beaded bacilli — is the classic presentation of pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB).

Causative organism: Mycobacterium tuberculosis — an acid-fast, obligate aerobe, non-motile, non-spore-forming, slow-growing (generation time 18–24 h) bacillus of family Mycobacteriaceae. The characteristic acid-fastness (red bacilli on Ziehl-Neelsen stain; auramine-rhodamine fluorescent on auramine O) is due to high mycolic acid content in the cell wall. Other components — arabinogalactan, peptidoglycan, lipoarabinomannan (LAM), wax D, phenolic glycolipid — make the wall impervious to Gram stain.

Other mycobacteria causing TB-like disease: M. bovis (unpasteurised milk), M. africanum (West Africa), M. microti (rodents). M. canettii. These are grouped as M. tuberculosis complex. Non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) — M. avium-intracellulare, M. kansasii, M. abscessus — cause opportunistic infection in immunocompromised.

(B) Pathogenesis (6 marks)

1. Source & Transmission

  • Source — open (sputum-positive) pulmonary TB case. Untreated smear-positive patient infects ~10–15 contacts/year.
  • Transmission — airborne droplet nuclei (1–5 µm) generated by coughing, sneezing, singing; remain suspended for hours; inhaled into terminal alveoli. NOT spread by fomites, food, or casual contact.
  • Infective dose — as few as 1–10 bacilli.
  • Incubation — 2–10 weeks for primary infection; years for reactivation.
  • Risk factors for infection & disease — HIV (highest risk — 5–15% annual risk of TB vs 5–15% lifetime in HIV-negative), malnutrition, diabetes, silicosis, smoking, immunosuppression (anti-TNF, steroids, transplant), chronic renal failure, malignancy, poverty, overcrowding.

2. Entry & Primary Infection (Ghon Complex)

  1. Inhalation — droplet nuclei reach terminal bronchioles & alveoli (upper lobe preferred — high oxygen tension).
  2. Phagocytosis by alveolar macrophages — bacilli ingested but resist killing due to:
    • Cell wall mycolic acid prevents fusion of phagosome with lysosome.
    • Trehalose dimycolate ("cord factor") causes serpentine cording & inhibits macrophage function.
    • Lipoarabinomannan (LAM) blocks macrophage activation, scavenges ROS, induces TNF-α.
    • Phagosome maturation arrest (blocks Rab5 → Rab7 conversion; retains TACO protein).
  3. Intracellular multiplication — bacilli multiply within macrophages; macrophage eventually ruptures, releasing bacilli to infect new macrophages.
  4. Dendritic cell migration — bacilli & antigen carried to draining hilar lymph nodes; presented to naïve T cells → CMI develops in 2–6 weeks.
  5. Granuloma formation
    • Activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), Langhans giant cells (multinucleated), CD4+ T cells (Th1), CD8+ T cells, B cells, fibroblasts.
    • Central caseous necrosis (cheese-like; due to TNF-α, IFN-γ, ischaemia).
    • Fibrosis & calcification contain the bacilli; bacilli dormant but viable for years.
  6. Ghon complex — subpleural parenchymal lesion (Ghon focus) + draining hilar lymph node involvement. Heals by fibrosis & calcification (Ranke complex). Visible on chest X-ray as calcified nodule.

3. Latent TB Infection (LTBI)

  • After primary infection, CMI contains the bacilli in granulomas; patient is asymptomatic, not infectious, but infected.
  • Tuberculin skin test (Mantoux) positive; IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold) positive.
  • Lifetime risk of reactivation ~5–10% in immunocompetent; 5–15% per year in HIV.
  • Reactivation typically in upper lobes (high oxygen tension).

4. Post-Primary (Adult/Reactivation) TB

  • Occurs years–decades after primary infection; due to waning immunity or new infection.
  • Location — apical & posterior segments of upper lobes (85%); superior segment of lower lobe (10%).
  • Pathology
    • Caseous necrosis with cavitation — erosion into bronchus allows bacilli to be coughed up (sputum positive; highly infectious).
    • Fibrocaseous lesions; endobronchial TB; haematogenous spread (miliary TB).
  • Immunology — Th1 cytokines (IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-2); CD8+ CTL killing; DTH reaction. TNF-α is critical for granuloma maintenance — anti-TNF therapy (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept) reactivates TB.

5. Spread

  • Local — endobronchial spread to other lobes (leading to "aspiration pneumonia" pattern).
  • Lymphatic — hilar, mediastinal, cervical lymph nodes (scrofuloderma).
  • Haematogenous — miliary TB (lung, liver, spleen, bone marrow, meninges); solitary extrapulmonary sites (Pott's spine, TB meningitis, GI, renal, pericardial, adrenal — Addison's).
  • Direct extension — pleural effusion, empyema, pericarditis, Pott's spine.

6. Pathological Stages

  1. Exudative — acute inflammation, exudate in alveoli; neutrophil & macrophage infiltrate.
  2. Caseative — caseous necrosis; epithelioid & giant cells; central cheesy material.
  3. Fibrocaseous — fibrosis surrounds caseum; cavity formation.
  4. Fibrous / calcified — healed lesion.

(C) Laboratory Diagnosis (7 marks)

1. Specimen Collection

  • Sputum — early morning, deep cough specimen (≥3 mL); 3 samples (spot-morning-spot or 3 consecutive mornings).
  • Induced sputum — hypertonic saline nebulisation for patients who cannot expectorate.
  • Bronchoscopy — bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), transbronchial biopsy for smear-negative.
  • Gastric lavage — early morning; for children <5 yr who swallow sputum (cannot expectorate); aspirate overnight-swallowed sputum from stomach.
  • Other specimens — CSF (TB meningitis), urine (renal TB), pleural fluid, pericardial fluid, ascitic fluid, synovial fluid, pus, tissue biopsy (lymph node, bone marrow, liver).
  • Transport — sterile wide-mouth container; refrigerate if delay >1 h; cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC) for transport if long delay.

2. Smear Microscopy

  • Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) stain — hot carbol fuchsin, acid-alcohol decolourisation, methylene blue counterstain. AFB appear red/pink against blue background.
  • Grading (WHO/RNTCP)
    • 3+ — >10 AFB per field (examine 20 fields).
    • 2+ — 1–10 AFB per field (50 fields).
    • 1+ — 10–99 AFB per 100 fields.
    • Scanty — 1–9 AFB per 100 fields (report exact number).
    • Negative — no AFB in 100 fields.
  • Sensitivity — 5,000–10,000 bacilli/mL sputum required for smear positivity; ~50–60% sensitivity vs culture. Negative smear does NOT exclude TB.
  • Auramine O (fluorescent stain) — yellow-orange bacilli on black background under UV; examine 40× objective (faster); preferred in high-burden settings.

3. Culture — Gold Standard

  • Solid media
    • Löwenstein-Jensen (LJ) — egg-based, malachite green (inhibits contaminants); colonies in 2–8 weeks (M. tuberculosis grows slowly — 18–24 h generation time).
    • Middlebrook 7H10/7H11 agar — faster (1–3 weeks).
  • Liquid culture (faster — 1–3 weeks)

    • VersaTREK.
  • Colony morphology — M. tuberculosis: buff-coloured, rough, dry, cauliflower-like colonies (cord factor causes serpentine growth); non-pigmented (photochromogen — M. kansasii; scotochromogen — M. scrofulaceum; non-chromogen — M. tuberculosis, M. avium).
  • Sensitivity — detects 10–100 bacilli/mL; gold standard for diagnosis; required for drug susceptibility testing.

4. Identification

  • Niacin test — M. tuberculosis produces niacin (positive); M. bovis negative.
  • Nitrate reduction — M. tuberculosis positive; M. bovis negative.
  • Catalase — variable; M. tuberculosis loses catalase at 68 °C (thermolabile).
  • Arylsulphatase — M. tuberculosis negative; M. fortuitum positive.
  • Tween 80 hydrolysis — M. tuberculosis positive (5 days); M. avium negative.
  • Pyrazinamidase — M. tuberculosis positive; M. bovis negative.
  • MTP40 antigen, MPT64 antigen — immunochromatographic rapid test (Capilia TB-Neo); confirms M. tuberculosis complex.
  • HPLC — mycolic acid pattern.
  • MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry — rapid identification.
  • Molecular — PCR (IS6110, 16S rRNA); line probe assay (GenoType MTBDRplus, MTBDRsl).

  • Cepheid Xpert MTB/RIF — automated real-time PCR; detects M. tuberculosis DNA + rifampicin resistance (rpoB gene mutations) in 2 hours.
  • Sensitivity — 90%+ in smear-positive; 70–80% in smear-negative; >95% specificity.
  • WHO-endorsed as first-line test for TB diagnosis (replaces smear microscopy in many settings).
  • Xpert Ultra — improved sensitivity (LOD 16 bacilli/mL vs 131 in MTB/RIF); useful in HIV, children, extrapulmonary TB.
  • Truenat MTB — Indian-made portable PCR; also detects rifampicin resistance.
  • Line Probe Assays (LPAs)
    • GenoType MTBDRplus — detects M. tuberculosis + rifampicin + isoniazid resistance (rpoB, katG, inhA).
    • GenoType MTBDRsl — second-line: fluoroquinolones (gyrA), aminoglycosides (rrs), ethambutol (embB) resistance.
    • Useful in MDR-TB diagnosis & management.
  • Whole Genome Sequencing (WGS) — comprehensive resistance profiling; research/specialised labs.

6. Tuberculin Skin Test (TST / Mantoux)

  • 5 TU PPD (purified protein derivative) intradermally on volar forearm; read induration at 48–72 h.
  • Positive — ≥5 mm (HIV, immunosuppressed, recent TB contact); ≥10 mm (healthcare workers, high-risk); ≥15 mm (low-risk general population).
  • Does NOT distinguish latent vs active TB; NOT diagnostic for active disease.
  • False positive — BCG vaccination, NTM infection.
  • False negative — anergy (HIV, malnutrition, measles, immunosuppression, military TB, severe active TB).

  • QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus (QFT-Plus) — ELISA measuring IFN-γ released by T cells in response to ESAT-6 & CFP-10 antigens (absent from BCG & most NTM).
  • T-SPOT.TB — ELISPOT counting IFN-γ-producing T cells.

  • First-line drugs tested — rifampicin (rpoB), isoniazid (katG, inhA), pyrazinamide (pncA), ethambutol (embB), streptomycin (rpsL, rrs, gidB).

  • HIV test — mandatory in every TB patient.

TB is the leading cause of death in people living with HIV — screen every HIV-positive patient for TB at every visit (4-symptom screen: cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss); if positive, send CBNAAT. The WHO goal of ending TB by 2030 (Sustainable Development Goal 3.3) requires intensified case finding, universal DST, MDR-TB scale-up, and TB preventive treatment.

The clinical picture — 7-year-old unimmunised child with high-grade fever, toxicity, severe sore throat, inability to swallow, and white patch on the fauces that bleeds when touched — is the classic presentation of pharyngeal diphtheria.

Corynebacterium diphtheriae — a Gram-positive, non-spore-forming, non-motile, non-capsulated pleomorphic bacillus.   • gravis — large, grey, daisy-head colonies; most severe; associated with epidemics.
  • intermedius — small, flat, black colonies; intermediate severity.
  • mitis — small, glossy, black colonies; mildest; common in endemic areas.
  • belfanti — non-lipophilic variant.

Toxigenic strains carry the tox gene (encoded by corynephage β — a lysogenic bacteriophage); non-toxigenic strains cause mild pharyngitis but not classic diphtheria. Only toxigenic strains produce diphtheria toxin.

1. Source & Transmission

  • Source — cases (symptomatic) & asymptomatic carriers (nasopharyngeal colonisation).
  • Transmission — droplet (coughing, sneezing); direct contact with wound exudate (cutaneous diphtheria); fomites (rare).
  • Incubation — 2–5 days (range 1–10 days).
  • Risk factors — unimmunised or incompletely immunised child; overcrowding; poor nutrition; immunocompromise; travel to endemic area.

  1. Adherence — via pili & surface proteins (DIP0733, DIP1281); C. diphtheriae colonises mucosa of tonsils, pharynx, larynx, nose; occasionally conjunctiva, genital mucosa, or skin (cutaneous diphtheria in tropics).
  2. Local invasion — bacteria remain superficial; do NOT invade deeper tissues or bloodstream.
  3. Pseudomembrane formation — bacteria + necrotic epithelial cells + fibrin + neutrophils + RBCs form a tough, adherent, grey-white membrane. Bleeds on attempted removal — characteristic. Extends from tonsils → uvula → soft palate → pharynx → larynx → trachea (causing airway obstruction).

  • Structure — AB toxin; 62 kDa single polypeptide.
    • A subunit (Fragment A, 21 kDa) — active catalytic moiety; released by proteolytic cleavage of disulfide bond.
    • B subunit (Fragment B, 41 kDa) — binding & translocation; binds heparin-binding epidermal growth factor-like (HB-EGF) receptor on host cells.
  • Cell entry
    1. B subunit binds HB-EGF receptor (all nucleated cells express; heart, nerves, kidneys particularly sensitive).
    2. Receptor-mediated endocytosis → endosome.

    4. A subunit translocates through pore into cytoplasm.
    5. Disulfide bond reduced → A subunit released.

  • Thermostable nuclease — positive; heat-resistant DNase (100 °C × 15 min); specific for S. aureus.
  • Phosphatase test — positive.
  • Novobiocin sensitivity — S. aureus sensitive; S. saprophyticus resistant (differentiates CoNS).
  • Polymyxin B (300 U) sensitivity — S. aureus sensitive; S. epidermidis resistant.
  • Baird-Parker agar — black shiny colonies with clear zone (egg yolk + tellurite).
  • MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry — rapid identification.
  • Molecular — PCR (nuc gene, femA; 16S rRNA); PBP2a latex agglutination for MRSA detection; mecA PCR; SCCmec typing.

5. Antibiotic Susceptibility Testing (AST)

  • Kirby-Bauer disk diffusion (CLSI/EUCAST breakpoints) — cefoxitin disc (30 µg) screen for MRSA; oxacillin MIC.
  • Automated — Vitek 2, Phoenix, MicroScan.
  • MRSA detection
    • Cefoxitin disc diffusion — ≤21 mm = MRSA.
    • Oxacillin MIC — ≥4 µg/mL = MRSA.
    • PBP2a latex agglutination — detects altered PBP in cell lysate.
    • mecA PCR — gold standard; detects resistance gene.
    • Chromogenic MRSA agar — direct detection in screening swabs; pink-mauve colonies.
  • Vancomycin
    • MIC — ≤2 µg/mL susceptible; 4–8 = VISA (vancomycin-intermediate); ≥16 = VRSA (vancomycin-resistant).
    • Vancomycin agar screen plate (6 µg/mL BHI).
  • Inducible clindamycin resistance (D-test) — erythromycin disc adjacent to clindamycin disc; flattening of clindamycin zone (D-shape) = positive; report clindamycin resistant.

Treatment

  • MSSA (methicillin-sensitive)
    • Flucloxacillin / dicloxacillin / cloxacillin 500 mg PO QID × 7 days — minor skin infection.
    • IV Nafcillin / Oxacillin 2 g 4-hourly — serious infection (endocarditis, osteomyelitis).
    • Cefazolin 2 g IV 8-hourly — alternative.
  • MRSA
    • Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV 12-hourly — drug of choice (monitor trough 15–20 µg/mL).
    • Teicoplanin — alternative glycopeptide.
    • Linezolid 600 mg IV/PO 12-hourly — VAP, SSI; excellent tissue penetration; watch for thrombocytopenia & lactic acidosis (>14 days).
    • Daptomycin 6–10 mg/kg IV daily — bacteraemia, endocarditis; NOT for pneumonia (inactivated by surfactant).
    • Ceftaroline 600 mg IV 12-hourly — only β-lactam active against MRSA.
    • Telavancin, Dalbavancin, Oritavancin — newer glycopeptides (single-dose option for skin/soft tissue).
    • Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, Doxycycline, Clindamycin — oral options for minor CA-MRSA skin infections.
  • Surgical drainage — for abscess, furuncle, carbuncle; may be sufficient alone for small abscesses.
  • Source control — remove infected catheter, device.

Prevention

  • Hand hygiene — most important.
  • Decolonisation — mupirocin nasal ointment + chlorhexidine body wash for MRSA carriers undergoing elective surgery, ICU admission, recurrent infection.
  • Contact precautions — isolation of MRSA-colonised patients; gown & gloves; dedicated equipment.
  • Active surveillance — nasal swab for MRSA on admission to ICU, high-risk units.
  • Antibiotic stewardship — limit unnecessary antibiotic use.
  • Vaccine — no licensed vaccine yet; candidates in trials.

Clinical Pearl

The coagulase test is the single most important laboratory test to differentiate S. aureus (coagulase-positive) from coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis, S. saprophyticus). The tube coagulase (free coagulase) test is the gold standard; the slide coagulase (bound coagulase/clumping factor) is a rapid screen. MRSA screening with cefoxitin disc or PBP2a latex agglutination or chromogenic agar is now standard before surgery & ICU admission. Panton-Valentine Leucocidin (PVL) is a marker of virulent CA-MRSA strains — associated with necrotising pneumonia (50% mortality), recurrent skin abscesses, and necrotising fasciitis. Vancomycin MIC creep (rising MICs over years within susceptible range) is a concern — alternative agents (daptomycin, linezolid, ceftaroline) are increasingly used. Always drain abscesses — antibiotics alone often fail because S. aureus forms abscess wall that antibiotics cannot penetrate. For native valve endocarditis, short-course therapy (2 weeks) with nafcillin + gentamicin is effective for uncomplicated right-sided endocarditis; left-sided disease requires 6 weeks. For S. aureus bacteraemia, repeat blood cultures every 48–72 h until negative; remove infected catheters; echo to exclude endocarditis; treat for 4–6 weeks minimum.
